In [[mathematics]], the '''blancmange curve''' is a [[self-affinity|self-affine]] [[fractal curve]] constructible by midpoint subdivision. It is also known as the  '''Takagi curve''', after [[Teiji Takagi]] who described it in 1901, or as the '''Takagi–Landsberg curve''', a generalization of the curve named after Takagi and [[Georg Landsberg]]. The name ''blancmange'' comes from its resemblance to a [[Blancmange|blancmange pudding]]. It is a special case of the more general [[de Rham curve]].

== Definition ==
The blancmange function is defined on the [[unit interval]] by

: <math>\operatorname{blanc}(x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty {s(2^{n}x)\over 2^n},</math>

where <math>s(x)</math> is the [[triangle wave]], defined by <math>s(x)=\min_{n\in{\mathbf Z}}|x-n|</math>,
that is, <math>s(x)</math> is the distance from ''x'' to the nearest [[integer]].

The Takagi–Landsberg curve is a slight generalization, given by

: <math>T_w(x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty w^n s(2^{n}x)</math>

for a parameter <math>w</math>; thus the blancmange curve is the case <math>w=1/2</math>. The value <math>H=-\log_2 w</math> is known as the [[Hurst parameter]].

The function can be extended to all of the real line: applying the definition given above shows that the function repeats on each unit interval.

=== Functional equation definition ===
The periodic version of the Takagi curve can also be defined as the ''unique bounded solution <math>T=T_w:\R\to\R</math> to the functional equation''

: <math>T(x) = s(x) + w T(2x).</math>

Indeed, the blancmange function <math>T_w</math> is certainly bounded, and solves the functional equation, since 
:<math> T_w(x) := \sum_{n=0}^\infty w^n s(2^{n}x)= s(x) + \sum_{n=1}^\infty w^n s(2^{n}x)</math><math> = s(x) + w\sum_{n=0}^\infty w^n s(2^{n+1}x)= s(x) + wT_w(2x). </math>
Conversely, if <math>T:\R\to\R</math> is a bounded solution of the functional equation, iterating the equality one has for any  ''N''
: <math>T(x) =\sum_{n=0}^N w^n s(2^n x) + w^{N+1} T(2^{N+1}x) =\sum_{n=0}^N w^n s(2^n x) + o(1), \text{ for } N\to\infty,</math> 

whence <math>T=T_w</math>. Incidentally, the above functional equations possesses infinitely many continuous, non-bounded solutions, e.g.
<math>T_w(x)+ c |x|^{-\log_2 w }.</math>

==Properties==

===Convergence and continuity===
The infinite sum defining <math>T_w(x)</math> [[absolute convergence|converges absolutely]] for all <math>x.</math> Since <math>0\le s(x) \le 1/2</math> for all <math>x\in \mathbb{R},</math>

:<math>\sum_{n=0}^\infty |w^n s(2^n x)| \le \frac{1}{2} \sum_{n=0}^\infty |w|^n = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{1-|w|}</math>

if <math>|w|<1.</math> The Takagi curve of parameter <math>w</math> is defined on the unit interval (or <math>\mathbb{R}</math>) if <math>|w|<1</math>. The Takagi function of parameter <math> w </math> is [[Continuous function|continuous]]. The functions <math>T_{w,n}</math> defined by the partial sums 

:<math>T_{w,n}(x) = \sum_{k=0}^n w^k s(2^k x)</math>

are continuous and [[Uniform convergence|converge uniformly]] toward <math>T_w:</math>

:<math>\begin{align}
\left|T_w(x) - T_{w,n}(x)\right|
& = \left|\sum_{k=n+1}^\infty w^k s(2^k x)\right| \\
& = \left|w^{n+1} \sum_{k=0}^\infty w^k s(2^{k+n+1} x)\right| \\
&\le \frac{|w|^{n+1}}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{1-|w|} \end{align}</math>

for all ''x'' when <math>|w| < 1. </math> This bound decreases as <math>n\to\infty.</math> By the [[uniform limit theorem]], <math>T_w</math> is continuous if |''w''|&nbsp;<&nbsp;1.

===Subadditivity===
Since the absolute value is a [[subadditive function]] so is the function <math>s(x)=\min_{n\in{\mathbf Z}}|x-n|</math>, and its dilations <math>s(2^kx)</math>; since positive linear combinations and point-wise limits of subadditive functions are subadditive, the Takagi function is subadditive for any value of the parameter <math> w </math>.

===The special case of the parabola===
For <math>w=1/4</math>, one obtains the [[parabola]]: the construction of the parabola by midpoint subdivision was described by [[Archimedes]].

===Differentiability===

For values of the parameter <math>0< w < 1/2,</math> the Takagi function <math>T_w</math>  is differentiable in the classical sense at any <math>x\in\R</math> which is not a [[dyadic rational]]. By derivation under the sign of series, for any non dyadic rational <math>x\in\R,</math> one finds

:<math>T_w^\prime(x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty (2w)^n \,(2b_n-1) </math>

where <math>(b_n)_{n\in\N}\in\{0,1\}^\N</math> is the sequence of binary digits in the [[base 2]] expansion of <math>x</math>:

:<math>x=\sum_{n=-k}^\infty b_n2^{-n-1}\;.</math>

Equivalently, the bits in the binary expansion can be understood as a sequence of [[Square wave (waveform)|square wave]]s, the [[Haar wavelet]]s, scaled to width <math>2^{-n}.</math> This follows, since the derivative of the triangle wave is just the square wave:

:<math>\frac{d}{dx}s(x)=\sgn( 1/2- (x \!\!\! \mod 1))</math>

and so

:<math>T_w^\prime(x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty (2w)^n \sgn (1/2-(2^nx \!\!\!\mod 1))</math>

For the parameter <math>0< w < 1/2,</math> the function  <math>T_w</math> is [[Lipschitz continuity|Lipschitz]] of constant <math>1/(1-2w).</math> In particular for the special value <math>w=1/4</math> one finds, for any non dyadic rational <math>x\in[0,1]</math> <math>T_{1/4}'(x) = 2 - 4x </math>, according with the mentioned  <math>T_{1/4}(x) = 2x(1 - x).</math>

For <math>w=1/2</math> the blancmange function <math>T_w</math> it is of [[bounded variation]]  on no non-empty open set; it is not even locally Lipschitz, but it is  quasi-Lipschitz, indeed, it admits the function  <math>\omega(t):=t(|\log_2 t| +1/2)</math> as a [[modulus of continuity]].

=== Fourier series expansion ===
The Takagi–Landsberg function admits an absolutely convergent Fourier series expansion: 
:<math>T_w(x) =\sum_{m=0}^\infty a_m\cos(2\pi m x) </math> 
with <math>a_0=1/4(1-w)</math> and, for <math>m\ge 1</math>
:<math>a_m:=-\frac{2}{\pi^2m^2}(4w)^{\nu(m)}, </math>
where <math>2^{\nu(m)}</math> is the maximum power of <math>2</math> that divides <math>m</math>.
Indeed, the  above [[triangle wave]] <math>s(x)</math> has an absolutely convergent Fourier series expansion
:<math>s(x)=\frac{1}{4}-\frac{2}{\pi^2}\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{1}{(2k+1)^2}\cos\big(2\pi (2k+1)x\big).</math>
By absolute convergence, one can reorder the corresponding double series for <math>T_w(x)</math>:

:<math>T_w(x):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty w^n s(2^nx)= \frac{1}{4}\sum_{n=0}^\infty w^n -\frac{2}{\pi^2}\sum_{n=0}^\infty\sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{w^n}{ (2k+1)^2}\cos\big(2\pi 2^n(2k+1)x\big)\, :</math>

putting <math>m=2^n(2k+1)</math> yields the above Fourier series for <math>T_w(x).</math>

=== Self similarity ===
The [[#recursive definition|recursive definition]] allows the [[monoid]] of self-symmetries of the curve to be given. This monoid is given by two generators, ''g'' and ''r'', which [[Group action (mathematics)|act]] on the curve (restricted to the unit interval) as

: <math>[g \cdot T_w](x) = T_w \left(g \cdot x\right)= T_w\left(\frac{x}{2}\right) = \frac{x}{2} + w T_w(x)</math>
and

: <math>[r \cdot T_w](x) = T_w(r \cdot x)  = T_w(1-x) = T_w(x). </math>

A general element of the monoid then has the form <math>\gamma=g^{a_1} r g^{a_2} r \cdots r g^{a_n}</math> for some integers <math>a_1, a_2, \cdots, a_n</math> This [[Group action (mathematics)|acts]] on the curve as a [[linear function]]: <math>\gamma \cdot T_w = a + bx + cT_w</math> for some constants ''a'', ''b'' and ''c''. Because the action is linear, it can be described in terms of a [[vector space]], with the [[vector space basis]]:

:<math>1 \mapsto e_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}</math>
:<math>x \mapsto e_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}</math>
:<math>T_w \mapsto e_3 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}</math>

In this [[Group representation|representation]], the action of ''g'' and ''r'' are given by

:<math>g=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & w \end{bmatrix}</math>
and
:<math>r=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}</math>

That is, the action of a general element <math>\gamma</math> maps the blancmange curve on the unit interval [0,1] to a sub-interval <math>[m/2^p, n/2^p]</math> for some integers ''m'', ''n'', ''p''. The mapping is given exactly by <math>[\gamma \cdot T_w](x) = a + bx + cT_w(x)</math> where the values of ''a'', ''b'' and ''c'' can be obtained directly by multiplying out the above matrices. That is:

:<math>\gamma=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & \frac{m}{2^p} & a \\ 0 & \frac{n-m}{2^p} & b \\ 0 & 0 & c \end{bmatrix}</math>

Note that <math>p=a_1+a_2+\cdots +a_n</math> is immediate.

The monoid generated by ''g'' and ''r'' is sometimes called the '''dyadic monoid'''; it is a sub-monoid of the [[modular group]].  When discussing the modular group, the more common notation for ''g'' and ''r'' is ''T'' and ''S'', but that notation conflicts with the symbols used here.

The above three-dimensional representation is just one of many representations it can have; it shows that the blancmange curve is one possible realization of the action.  That is, there are representations for  any dimension, not just 3; some of these give the [[de Rham curve]]s.

==Integrating the Blancmange curve==
Given that the [[integral]] of <math>\operatorname{blanc}(x)</math> from 0 to 1 is 1/2, the identity <math>\operatorname{blanc}(x)= \operatorname{blanc}(2x)/2+s(x)</math> allows the integral over any interval to be computed by the following relation. The computation is recursive with computing time on the order of log of the accuracy required. Defining

:<math>I(x) = \int_0^x\operatorname{blanc}(y)\,dy</math>
one has that
:<math>I(x) =\begin{cases}
I(2x)/4+x^2/2 & \text{if } 0 \leq x \leq 1/2  \\
1/2-I(1-x) & \text{if } 1/2 \le x \le 1 \\
n/2+I(x-n) & \text{if } n \le x \le (n+1) \\
\end{cases}</math>
The [[definite integral]] is given by:
:<math>\int_a^b\operatorname{blanc}(y)\,dy = I(b) - I(a).</math>

A more general expression can be obtained by defining
:<math>S(x)=\int_0^x s(y)dy = \begin{cases} 
  x^2/ 2,  & 0 \le x \le \frac{1}{2} \\ 
  - x^2 / 2 +x - 1/4,  & \frac{1}{2} \le x \le 1 \\
  n/4 + S(x-n), & (n \le x \le n+1)
\end{cases}</math>
which, combined with the series representation, gives

:<math>I_w(x)= \int_0^x T_w(y) dy = \sum_{n=0}^\infty (w/2)^n S(2^n x)</math>

Note that
:<math>I_w(1)=\frac{1}{4(1-w)}</math>

This integral is also self-similar on the unit interval, under an action of the dyadic monoid described in the section ''[[#Self similarity|Self similarity]]''. Here, the representation is 4-dimensional, having the basis <math>\{e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4\}=\{1, x, x^2, I_w(x)\}</math>.  The action of ''g'' on the unit interval is the [[commuting diagram]]

:<math>[g\cdot I_w](x) = I_w\left(g \cdot x\right) = I_w\left(\frac{x}{2}\right) = \frac{x^2}{8} + \frac{w}{2}I_w(x). </math>

From this, one can then immediately read off the [[generating set of a group|generators]] of the four-dimensional representation:

:<math>g=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 
  0 & 0 & \frac{1}{4} & \frac{1}{8} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \frac{w}{2} \end{bmatrix}</math>
and
:<math>r=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 & \frac{1}{4(1-w)} \\ 0 & -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 
      0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}</math>

Repeated integrals transform under a 5,6,... dimensional representation.

== Relation to simplicial complexes ==
Let
: <math> N=\binom{n_t}{t}+\binom{n_{t-1}}{t-1}+\ldots+\binom{n_j}{j},\quad
n_t > n_{t-1} > \ldots > n_j \geq j\geq 1. </math>

Define the Kruskal–Katona function

:<math>
\kappa_t(N)={n_t \choose t+1} + {n_{t-1} \choose t} + \dots + {n_j \choose j+1}.
</math>

The [[Kruskal–Katona theorem]] states that this is the minimum number of (''t''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1)-simplexes that are faces of a set of ''N'' ''t''-simplexes.

As ''t'' and ''N'' approach infinity,
<math> \kappa_t(N)-N </math> (suitably normalized) approaches the blancmange curve.
